narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank near the middle of their class. This low ranking signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction somewhat toward passing. At 3.00 it sits only modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, giving the model a small positive signal.

Your LSAT score of 30 was the third most influential feature and again nudged the outcome toward failure. It falls noticeably short of the 37-point average among students who were admitted.

Taken together, the model concluded your academic performance so far makes success on the bar exam more likely to be difficult. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining law school years and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. These two steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (248 words)
